implementation_notes: JavaFX owns the frame cadence: an AnimationTimer is 'a timer, that is called in each frame while it is active', its handle(long now) 'will be called in every frame', and the timestamp is 'the timestamp of the current frame given in nanoseconds', identical for all timers polled in one frame. What replaces the classic structure: the toolkit's pulse replaces the driver loop and the sleep - implement handle, accumulate now deltas into a lag value and step a fixed dt inside it; start() and stop() begin and end the loop. Long work inside handle runs on the JavaFX application thread and stalls the pulse, so per-frame work must stay inside the frame budget. libGDX's ApplicationListener.render(float delta) is the same shape for JVM games; for headless simulations use the manual nanoTime loop instead, because no toolkit pulse exists there.
pitfalls: handle runs on the JavaFX application thread, so blocking I/O, sleeps or long computation inside it freeze the UI and the pulse - move work off-thread and hand results back.
The now argument is the frame timestamp; mixing it with freshly sampled System.nanoTime() values is redundant and can mis-order measurements - pick one clock for the accumulator.
AnimationTimer has no fixed update rate; the pulse rate is toolkit-controlled, so a fixed step must be accumulated from now deltas rather than assumed per call.
Do not mutate the scene graph from other threads: marshal changes with Platform.runLater or the pulse and the mutation race.

variants.name: Hand-written System.nanoTime loop
variants.implementation_notes: On the JVM itself, System.nanoTime 'returns the current value of the running Java Virtual Machine's high-resolution time source, in nanoseconds' and 'can only be used to measure elapsed time and is not related to any other notion of system or wall-clock time' - exactly what the loop needs, and the reason System.currentTimeMillis is the wrong clock for intervals. Thread.sleep 'causes the currently executing thread to sleep ... for the specified number of milliseconds, subject to the precision and accuracy of system timers and schedulers', so it is at-least timing and the loop must re-read nanoTime afterwards. What replaces the classic structure: nothing - the driver, accumulator and clamp are hand-written; this is the correct realization for dedicated servers, headless simulations, CLI tools and tests, where no toolkit pulse exists.
variants.idiom_name: System.nanoTime delta accumulator with Thread.sleep pacing
pitfalls: System.currentTimeMillis is wall-clock time and jumps when the system clock is corrected; only nanoTime differences are meaningful for intervals.
Thread.sleep can oversleep and throws InterruptedException (clearing the interrupt flag); treat the sleep as a hint and keep the loop's own timing authoritative.
nanoTime spans roughly 292 years before wrapping, but converting to double seconds loses precision over long sessions: subtract in long nanoseconds as above.
A dedicated loop thread mutating shared world state needs synchronization or an ownership rule; the Java memory model gives no visibility guarantees without one.
